_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning to interpret network diagrams that represent real-world relationships and describe their features.

_source.w: We are learning to interpret network diagrams that represent real-world relationships and describe their features.
y: Network (graph) theory provides tools for analysing connections and pathways — it is one of the most widely applied branches of modern mathematics.
Understanding networks helps us model and optimise transportation, social connections, communication systems and resource distribution.
These concepts connect mathematics to computer science, logistics, urban planning and epidemiology.
eg: Interpreting a network diagram showing flight routes between cities and identifying the shortest path.
Describing networks using mathematical language: nodes/vertices, edges, degree, connected graphs.
Determining whether an Euler path or circuit exists in a given network.
Modelling a social network and identifying the most connected individuals (highest degree nodes).
Using a network diagram to model and optimise a delivery route.
Identifying whether a network is planar (can be drawn without crossing edges).

toLevel2.question: A vertex in a network represents a connection or edge between nodes.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A vertex represents a node or connection point. Edges represent the connections between vertices.

distractors.explanation: Vertices are nodes; edges are the connections between them.

toLevel2.question: The degree of a vertex is the number of vertices in the network.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The degree of a vertex is the number of edges connected to it, not the total number of vertices.

distractors.explanation: Degree counts all vertices in the network.

toLevel2.question: An edge in a network represents a connection between two vertices.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Edges (arcs, links) connect pairs of vertices and represent relationships.

distractors.explanation: An edge is another name for a vertex in a network.

toLevel2.question: The sum of all vertex degrees in a network equals the number of edges.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The sum of degrees equals twice the number of edges, because each edge contributes to the degree of two vertices.

distractors.explanation: Each edge adds one to the degree sum, so they are equal.

toLevel2.question: A connected network has a path between every pair of vertices.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Connectedness means any vertex can be reached from any other vertex through some sequence of edges.

distractors.explanation: A connected network only requires some vertices to be reachable.

toLevel2.question: Two network diagrams that look different must represent different networks.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Networks are defined by their connections, not their visual layout. Different diagrams can represent identical networks.

distractors.explanation: The appearance of the diagram determines which network it represents.

toLevel2.question: A tree is a connected network that contains no circuits.

distractors.explanation: Trees can contain circuits as long as they are connected.

distractors.explanation: A loop counts as a single connection, adding 1 to the degree.
